$comment: Definitive rejection versus transient failure: does a failed refresh mean the stored
credential is dead, or only that the platform could not answer right now?
This is the one auth decision whose two failure modes are not symmetric. Reading a
transient failure as definitive throws away a working session over a dropped packet.
Reading a definitive rejection as transient retries a dead credential at every launch,
fails silently each time, and never asks for the sign-in that would fix it. Only the
second is silent, so everything unrecognised is transient.
Both registered hosts implemented this independently and identically before it was lifted
here. That agreement is the thing this case exists to keep: the codes below are a platform
contract, and a host that adds a fifth spelling locally has forked the contract.
matrixNote: Every codeKey x definitiveCode pair at matrixStatus must classify as definitive. The cross product is the point: each host had a hand-written table that covered a diagonal of it.

vectors.note: 401 is the other client-error status that can carry a verdict
a 5xx is never definitive whatever the body says - the platform is not answering, and its proxy may have written this body
a success status is not a rejection at all
a client error with an unrecognised code is transient - back off, do not discard
prose is not a verdict. error_description changes between platform versions, and matching on it is how this check quietly stops working
a definitive code nested one level down is not this key's value; a reader that searches the body rather than reading the field would fail here
an unreadable body is transient - a proxy error page lands here with a client-error status
valid JSON that is not an object. The definitive code is present as text, so a reader doing a substring search over the body reports this as definitive and discards a live credential
